## Research design

The study examines two potential sources of improvement in portfolio tail-risk
forecasting: conditional volatility and cross-asset dependence. Direct portfolio
benchmarks establish the performance of simpler forecasts, including a univariate
GARCH-t model. Copula comparisons then hold the conditional marginal forecasts fixed
and vary the dependence specification. Rolling out-of-sample evaluation measures
both tail calibration and predictive loss.

## Data and valuation calendar

Daily source prices are restricted to the configured inclusive date range and asset
set. Weekly observations use a common Friday valuation calendar. Each asset is valued
at its latest quote available by the cutoff, with a maximum configured age of zero
to four calendar days. Admissible weekly observations therefore contain a quote from
the same calendar week for every asset. The sample ends with the last complete week;
daily profiles instead use common observed trading dates.

The valuation audit records each cutoff, asset, quote date, quote age and price.
Weekly valuation dates are exactly seven days apart, while quote ages accommodate
differences in market holidays. This construction represents daily closing-price
information rather than intraday synchronization. Synthetic fixtures use Friday
dates and support software verification separately from the empirical experiment.

## Portfolio returns and tail-risk measures

Let $R_{i,t}$ denote the simple return on asset $i$ and $w_i$ its fixed weight.
Portfolio simple return is $R_{p,t}=\sum_i w_i R_{i,t}$, and portfolio log return is
$\log(1+R_{p,t})$. Both simulated and observed portfolio returns use this aggregation
and the same configured return convention. Maintaining fixed weights implies
rebalancing at each observation; the experiment abstracts from trading costs.

Under the local-index-return convention, each index contributes its local-currency
return. A base-currency specification instead requires aligned FX returns quoted as
base-currency units per unit of asset currency.

For signed portfolio return $r$, define loss $L=-r$. At confidence $c$, VaR is the
$c$ quantile of loss, and ES averages the worst $1-c$ probability mass. The signed
outputs `loss_var` and `loss_es` enter scoring and exception calculations. They may
be negative when the relevant tail still earns a gain. The `var` and `es` columns
present their nonnegative display magnitudes.

For empirical ES, losses are ordered from largest to smallest. The largest
$\lfloor n(1-c)\rfloor$ observations receive full weight, and the next receives the
fractional remainder. Dividing their weighted sum by $n(1-c)$ gives the average over
exactly the desired tail mass. The definition applies to samples with tied values
and to samples smaller than $1/(1-c)$.

## Conditional marginals and dependence

Asset returns are represented as
$r_{i,t}=\mu_{i,t}+\sigma_{i,t}z_{i,t}$, combining an ARMA conditional mean with a
GARCH-family conditional variance and a selected innovation distribution. Marginal
specification selection combines convergence and parameter checks, residual and
squared-residual Ljung–Box diagnostics, and AIC/BIC ranking. When no candidate passes
every diagnostic screen, the best valid converged specification is retained with
its fallback status.

Probability integral transforms map standardized innovations into marginal uniforms.
PIT KS/AD statistics describe the fitted residual distributions. Their conventional
p-values are exploratory because the marginal parameters are estimated from the
same observations; calibrated inference would require a refit-aware bootstrap or
an independently validated forecast sample. Values are clipped inside $(0,1)$ for
numerical inverse-CDF evaluation, and clipping counts are recorded.

The conditional copula combines these marginals into a joint forecast. This
decomposition permits volatility and marginal tail behaviour to be studied separately
from dependence, including asymmetric dependence [@patton2006]. Copula coefficients
are interpreted on the return-CDF scale: lower-tail dependence concerns joint extreme
losses, while upper-tail dependence concerns joint extreme gains.

Joint uniforms are transformed through the marginal inverse CDFs, conditional means
and volatilities are restored, and asset returns are aggregated in simple-return
space. Portfolio risk is then evaluated in the configured return space.

The native two-step marginal implementation provides a computational approximation.
Its information-criterion comparisons are restricted to the selected ARMA order.
The outputs identify the estimation engine, allowing this approximation to be
distinguished from the joint-likelihood production-package fits.

## Benchmarks and dependence comparisons

The benchmark set covers historical, Gaussian, Student-t, EWMA and
filtered-historical forecasts. A fixed univariate portfolio sGARCH(1,1) model with
Student-t innovations provides a conditional-volatility reference.

The dependence experiment compares independence, Gaussian, Student-t and BB1 copulas
using the same selected and refitted marginal forecasts at each origin. The main
copula-GARCH procedure selects its dependence family according to the configured
criterion. Comparing these forecasts isolates dependence assumptions, while the
comparison with portfolio GARCH-t measures the value of the full multivariate
construction. Unsuccessful fixed-family fits remain part of forecast-availability
accounting.

## Rolling forecasts and calibration

At origin $t$, estimation uses observations through $t$ and the forecast is evaluated
on the next valuation. Moving or expanding estimation windows and the specification
selection schedule are configuration choices. Selected specifications are refitted
at every origin.

Coverage statistics describe each model's available forecasts on the evaluation
calendar. The unconditional coverage test examines the exception frequency relative
to the nominal tail probability [@kupiec1995]. Independence and conditional coverage
also examine the ordering of exceptions [@christoffersen1998]. Transition counts use
adjacent available forecasts; an intervening missing forecast leaves a gap.
Boundary cases can leave independence unidentified.

Forecast-date, model and confidence-level combinations uniquely identify a forecast,
and all models share the realised return at a given date. Availability and failed
forecasts are reported together with calibration. Sparse expected tail exceptions
limit coverage-test power, so coverage results are interpreted alongside predictive
scores.

## Predictive loss and Expected Shortfall scoring

Quantile loss evaluates signed VaR forecasts. Each confidence-level comparison uses
the dates with valid scores for every included model. Mean joint VaR/ES scores use
their own common set, with sample counts and availability reported separately.
Ranks describe the ordering of observed mean losses.

Joint scoring assesses VaR and ES as a pair, following the evaluation framework
discussed by @pattonziegelchen2019. The implemented Fissler–Ziegel zero-homogeneous
score is

$$
S(L,v,e)=\frac{\max(L-v,0)}{(1-c)e}+\frac{v}{e}+\log(e)-1,
\qquad e>0,\quad e\geq v.
$$

Lower mean scores indicate better observed forecasts on the same sample and at the
same confidence level. Signed VaR may be negative. The positive-ES domain determines
which forecasts enter FZ0 comparisons: otherwise valid forecasts with nonpositive
signed ES have unavailable FZ0 scores. Descriptive tail residuals provide an
additional view of forecast errors conditional on exceedance; they are not a formal
ES hypothesis test.

## Paired inference and simulation precision

Paired comparisons use the same eligible dates across all models at each confidence
level and score type. Loss differences are model minus reference, so a negative
mean measures an observed predictive gain. A circular block bootstrap, with
$\lceil n^{1/3}\rceil$ observations per block by default, estimates uncertainty while
retaining local serial dependence. It reports a marginal percentile interval and a
centred two-sided bootstrap p-value. Holm adjustment applies across all comparisons
in the call; the percentile intervals remain marginal rather than simultaneous.

Inference requires at least 20 paired observations and at least two blocks. It is
reported for a contiguous common forecast sample. When internal calendar gaps or
limited observations preclude inference, the mean difference, sample fraction and
status remain available. Per-date score differences support examination of the
periods contributing to an aggregate gain or loss.

The magnitude of a mean loss reduction and its sampling uncertainty answer distinct
questions. An interval spanning zero leaves uncertainty about the persistence of
the observed gain. Evaluation-period selection, model selection and multiple
comparisons also affect how broadly a favourable result can be interpreted.

Repeated Monte Carlo seeds estimate simulation variation conditional on the fitted
parameters. They help assess the adequacy of the simulation budget, while parameter,
specification and regime uncertainty require separate analysis. Reproduction uses
the recorded seed, RNG kind, draw count and chunk size together.

## Reproducibility and scope

The experiment records source and configuration identities, input hashes, valuation
coverage, software versions and simulation settings. The local run archive contains
the price snapshot, configuration and session information. Checkpoint identities
also include the implementation, allowing a resumed experiment to retain its
estimation design. Output hashes connect the generated tables and figures to a
single recorded experiment.

The empirical design is bivariate and uses a fixed-weight index portfolio. Its
default local-index-return convention excludes FX hedging, transaction costs and
market microstructure effects. Results describe the observed out-of-sample period;
additional portfolios and market regimes provide further tests of the stability
and practical value of the measured forecasting gains.
